title: in the application by The Executors of Major John Carmichael Kirkpatrick Young Applicants against James Stewart Miller Respondent [2026] SLC 1
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 1,
Case reference: SLC/104/06

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr John Smith

in the application by
The Executors of Major John Carmichael Kirkpatrick Young
Applicants
against
James Stewart Miller
Respondent

The Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991

Applicants: Sutherland, advocate; Gillespie Macandrew LLP

Respondent: Upton, advocate; Holmes Mackillop

22 January 2026

Introduction

[1] This is an application by the landlord applicants under the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991 for an order declaring that the lease of Burnside and Flenders Farm, Clarkston, Glasgow, was validly terminated by a notice to quit dated 26 May 2006. The notice specifies termination at Martinmas 2007 in respect of the lands ploughed for crop and the lands in hay for that crop, and termination at Whitsunday 2008 in respect of the houses, yards and pastures. The application is opposed.

[2] The original tenant was Matthew Miller, who died on 29 May 2007. His son, James Stewart Miller, who is named as respondent in the instance, intimated acceptance of transfer of the tenant’s interest under section 12(1) of the 1991 Act. The applicants served a counter‑notice objecting to receiving him as tenant.

[3] The respondent invites the court, in light of the procedural history of this matter outlined below, to dismiss the application on the ground of inordinate, inexcusable and unfairly prejudicial delay by the applicants in progressing the application. The matter called for a debate on the respondent’s preliminary plea.

Procedural history

[4] The application was commenced in 2006. Following the death of Matthew Miller, James Stewart Miller gave the landlord notice on 21 May 2008 of his inheritance of the lease under section 12(1) of the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Act 1991. The landlord sent a counter‑notice but did not apply to this court for an order terminating the lease under section 12(2). After sundry procedure a proof was fixed. However, that proof was discharged and on 15 and 17 February 2010 parties executed a Minute of Agreement, which was registered in the Books of Council and Session on 18 February 2010. The agreement provides for dismissal of the application in consideration of surrender of the lease, sale of part of the holding to the tenant, grant of a limited‑duration tenancy over other parts, and provision for possible development. Clause 13 makes the agreement conditional on the obtaining of the consent of Mactaggart & Mickel as holder of an option and a standard security over the subjects. In the event, no agreement was reached with Mactaggart & Mickel. The application was sisted. No steps were taken to progress the application between January 2009 and December 2022.

[5] On 13 December 2022 the court ordained parties to lodge proposals for further procedure. Sundry procedure followed. Major Young died on 14 November 2024. His executors obtained confirmation on 7 July 2025, following which the court fixed a diet of debate.

Submissions for the respondent

[6] Counsel adopted his note of argument. Rule 1(4) of the Scottish Land Court Rules 2014 directs the court to have regard to practice in the sheriff court in making any order in relation to a matter not expressly provided for in those rules. The practice of the sheriff court and the Court of Session is to dismiss where there has been both inordinate and inexcusable delay together with an added element of unfairness in the relevant factual and procedural context: Macphail, Sheriff Court Practice, paragraphs 2-10; Newman Shopfitters Ltd v M.J. Gleeson Group plc 2003 SLT (Sh Ct) 83. Reference was also made to decisions of the Court of Session (which, counsel commented, follow the lead of the sheriff court in respect of the courts’ inherent, common‑law powers) as stated in Tonner v Reiach & Hall [2007] CSIH 48 and Hepburn v Royal Alexandra NHS Trust [2010] CSIH 71. Dismissal is justified only if the element of unfairness is such that there is a substantial risk that a fair trial is no longer possible: Hepburn, supra per Lord President Hamilton at [39] and Lord Reed at [51]. Whether there is such a risk is partly a function of the survival of evidence: Hepburn, supra per Lord President Hamilton at [42], [43]. In addition, a respondent has the right, in terms of Article 6(1) of the European Convention on Human Rights, to have his civil rights and obligations determined by the court “within a reasonable time”.

[7] The delay is inordinate. Nineteen years have passed since the application was lodged and 12 years since the conditional settlement agreement was entered into. No steps were taken to progress the application between January 2009 and December 2022. The prospect of further delay in the future is also relevant, particularly given defects in the landlord’s pleadings. If or when the application is admitted to proof, that could only be after a further period of time for amendment or adjustment of the pleadings. A proof would presumably take much of a week, after which there would be a period of avizandum and possibly a subsequent appeal, which would defer determination of the application until more than two decades after it was commenced.

[8] The delay is inexcusable. The applicants found on the late Major Young’s deteriorating health as meaning that he was not in a position to pursue the application. However, a power of attorney was in place since September 1996. By the time that the Minute of Agreement was entered into in February 2010, it recorded that James Alister Aitkenhead was acting as his attorney. It is no answer to a plea of inordinate, inexcusable and unfairly prejudicial delay that the respondent could have taken steps to progress matters. A respondent is subject to no such positive responsibility: Tonner, supra at [128]. Inexcusable delay remains inexcusable though caused by a pursuer’s solicitor: Wilson v Drake & Scull Scotland Ltd, 2005 SLT (Sh Ct) 35, at [20].

[9] There is a substantial risk that a fair trial is no longer possible. The pleadings refer to numerous oral discussions between 1986 and 2006. Five of the eight participants in those discussions have since passed on. The whereabouts of a sixth individual, Mr Alan Beckett, the contractor with whom the Millers discussed repairs in 1998, are unknown. The memories of the three surviving witnesses of conversations dating from 2006 back to 1986 will have deteriorated.

[10] Documentary evidence is absent for issues including rent reviews, repair costs and correspondence. There are several matters in respect of which it is either manifest or could reasonably be inferred that relevant documents existed between 1984 and 2007 but which have not been produced and are not available to the respondent, including documents pertaining to the respondent’s participation in rent reviews, complaints, the cost of storm damage repairs, and a letter written by the tenant in December 2005. The absence of such documents creates a substantial risk of unfairness and is, of itself, sufficient to justify dismissal.

[11] The applicants’ argument that the respondent has had the benefit of occupation without paying rent is irrelevant to the determinative issues of whether, in circumstances where there has been inordinate and inexcusable delay, there is a substantial risk that a fair trial is not possible. In any event, the respondent tendered rent, which was refused. Further, esto the landlord has been wrongly prejudiced by the respondent’s occupation of the farm (which is denied), that is because of his own failure to progress this case. Moreover, any claim for rent older than 5 years is extinguished by prescription.

[12] Dismissal accords with parties’ underlying, substantive rights. The application seeks to enforce a right to terminate for non-payment of rent in 2003. A right of rescission must be exercised within a reasonable time. Eighteen years is manifestly unreasonable.

Submissions for the applicants

[13] Counsel adopted his note of argument and supplementary note. Dismissal is a course of last resort and is not justified on the circumstances of the present case.

[14] Two applications between the same parties are in dependence before the court. The present application concerns the validity of termination of the tenancy. Application SLC/39/21 (raised by the tenant in 2021, and which seeks approval of tenant’s improvements in respect of the same subjects as the present proceedings) is sisted to await the outcome of this application. There is a substantial overlap between the two applications.

[15] In the present application a proof was fixed in 2010 but negotiations resulted in the 2010 Minute of Agreement. The respondent failed to implement its terms. The agreed sale of land and the creation of a limited duration tenancy did not proceed, nor were the associated option and security arrangements regularised. The respondent has remained in occupation throughout and no rent has been paid.

[16] Delay, even where substantial, is not of itself determinative of whether dismissal should be granted. Each case turns on its own circumstances. Dismissal requires a substantial risk that a fair trial cannot be held. Reference was made to Tonner, supra, Hepburn, supra, Abram v British International Helicopters Ltd 2015 SCLR 95 and Mannas v Chief Constable of Police Scotland 2019 SCLR 909. In the present case the delay is at least partly excusable and does not give rise to such unfairness. Any relevant delay should be assessed from late 2010, when it became apparent that the Minute of Agreement would not be implemented, until the death of Major Young in November 2024. From around 2014 onwards, Major Young’s deteriorating health and constrained financial position rendered him unable, in practical terms, to advance the litigation or to raise further proceedings.

[17] Despite the passage of time, a fair hearing remains possible. Determination of the issues is neither impossible nor impractical. Although some witnesses are no longer available, contemporaneous documentary records exist. Evidence is available from the former law agent and from Savills, whose directors have dealt with the estate for many years. James Stewart Miller has been directly involved throughout the relevant period and remains available to give evidence. Any disadvantage arising from the absence of witnesses falls more heavily on the applicants, who bear the onus of justifying the notices to quit.

[18] The applicants would suffer prejudice if the application were dismissed. The respondent has remained in occupation without paying rent and now advances claims for historic tenant’s improvements under a separate application. Dismissal would expose the applicants to potential liability for improvements which would not arise if the tenancy had been validly terminated. Any prejudice to the respondent arising from the delay is not so great as to justify dismissal. Application SLC/104/06 should be permitted to proceed to determination.

Decision

[19] We are satisfied that the delay in this application has been inordinate, inexcusable and has resulted in a substantial risk that a fair trial is no longer possible.

[20] The delay is inordinate. The application was raised in 2006. No procedural steps were taken between January 2009 and December 2022. More than 19 years have elapsed since commencement. More than a decade passed after the execution of the 2010 conditional Minute of Agreement during which no progress was made. If the application were now to proceed to proof, final determination will occur more than 20 years after proceedings were raised. Delay of that magnitude goes well beyond what is tolerable in civil litigation.

[21] The delay is inexcusable. A continuing power of attorney was in place since 1996. By February 2010 it was expressly recorded that Major Young was acting through an attorney. There was no legal impediment to procedural steps being taken on his behalf. Nor does the failure of the 2010 Minute of Agreement excuse subsequent inaction. It was apparent by late 2010 at the latest that the conditions for its implementation would not be met. No steps were taken thereafter for more than 12 years, and then only as a result of intervention by the court.

[22] The fact that the respondent did not seek to force progress does not render the delay excusable. A respondent is under no obligation to advance proceedings raised by another party. Delay remains inexcusable even where attributable to the actions of a party’s agents. Responsibility for progressing the application lay with the applicants.

[23] The delay has resulted in unfairness of such a degree that there is now a substantial risk that a fair hearing is no longer possible. Central issues in the application depend upon factual disputes concerning events spanning many years, including alleged oral discussions, rent reviews, repairs, set off arrangements and the circumstances said to justify termination for non‑payment of rent. Five of the eight individuals who participated in relevant discussions are now deceased. The whereabouts of a sixth individual are unknown. The remaining two witnesses would be required to recall conversations dating back as far as 1986. The inevitable deterioration of recollection over such a period materially undermines the reliability of any evidence now capable of being led.

[24] The position is not materially improved by reference to documentary evidence. There are significant gaps. Documents which one would reasonably expect to have existed, relating for example to rent reviews, repair costs, complaints, storm damage and correspondence in December 2005, are absent and appear no longer to be available. In circumstances where the application depends upon proof of historical facts, the loss of such material increases the risk of unfairness.

[25] The applicants’ submission that a fair trial remains possible because some witnesses and professional advisers are still available is unpersuasive. The question is not whether it is possible to hold a hearing, rather, whether there is a substantial risk that the court would be unable to determine the issues fairly. In our view that risk is now considerable. Any disadvantage arising from the absence of evidence may fall on either party, but that does not mitigate the unfairness inherent in requiring the respondent to resist these proceedings after such an excessive and unexplained delay.

[26] We have had regard to the prejudice said to arise if the application were dismissed, including the respondent’s continued occupation and the existence of a separate application for approval of improvements. Those matters do not outweigh the fundamental difficulty that the present proceedings can no longer be resolved fairly. The prejudice to the applicants is the result of the landlord’s own failure to bring matters to determination timeously.

[27] We will grant the respondent’s motion and dismiss the application. We appoint parties to submit any motions for expenses within 21 days of intimation of this decision.
